title: Festivals and everyday culture
job: Talk about what is happening around you
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Sāturnālia IS PLURAL AND HAS NO SINGULAR AT ALL: Sāturnālia sunt, never est. Latin has a small set of festival names that exist only in the plural, and this is where a learner meets the idea that a word can have no singular. L2-M9's tria verba prepared the neuter plural in -a; this is the same ending with nothing behind it. Nothing in the English 'the Saturnalia' warns you and nothing in the Latin word does either.

A BIRTHDAY IS 'THE DAY OF BEING BORN', TWO WORDS AGREEING: diēs nātālis. nātālis belongs to M2's two-shape family, so it looks the same for a man or a woman and tells you nothing about whose birthday it is — that has to come from somewhere else in the sentence, and this course has no plain possessive to supply it.

A CUSTOM IS mōs est PLUS AN INFINITIVE, WHICH IS M7's FRAME WITH A NOUN IN FRONT: mōs est dōna dare, 'it is the custom to give gifts'. Nothing about the structure is new — melius est built it two modules ago — so a ninth module spends its cap on nouns rather than on grammar, which is what a module this late should do.

THE CULTURE IN THIS MODULE IS ROMAN, AND THAT WAS DECIDED ONCE FOR THE WHOLE COURSE. Naming the learner's own festivals in Latin was rejected: docs/123 §7 allows exactly one named source for modern words, that source has a telephone and a bicycle in it and has no Diwali or Christmas Eve, and coining is banned everywhere in this course. So the module teaches Sāturnālia and diēs nātālis and says whose festivals they are. Same honesty L2-M7 needed for the telephone and M8 for the office, from the same source.

hodiē JOINS L1-M4's CASELESS SET AND NEVER TAKES AN ENDING: cotīdiē, crās, herī, hodiē. Four words that never decline, beside the time ablative L2-M6 and L3-M1 made productive (hōrā prīmā, hōrā sextā). The course now has two ways of saying when — one with a case and one without — and a learner who tries to put hodiē in the ablative has crossed them.

nōn DENIES WHATEVER IT STANDS IN FRONT OF, AND THIS MODULE PUTS TWO INFINITIVES BEHIND ONE et. mōs est dōna dare et nōn labōrāre — the custom is to give AND not to work, so nōn belongs to labōrāre alone. Moving it in front of dare would negate both, which is a different holiday; moving it in front of est would make working merely uncustomary. M7 and M8 each spent a plate on this.

mōs BECOMES mōrem IN A REPORTED CLAUSE, AND THE SENTENCE ENDS UP THREE VERBS DEEP: dīcit mōrem esse dōna dare. esse is the reported clause's own verb and dare is what the custom is — two infinitives doing two different jobs, and every shape in it taught earlier in the level. This is M5's construction at its most stacked.

A NEUTER PLURAL LOOKS UNCHANGED AFTER A PREPOSITION: ad Sāturnālia eō. M8 said the same about pretium in a reported clause — neuter nominative and accusative are identical — so a learner watching endings sees nothing move and the preposition is the only evidence the case changed. ut plus a subjunctive is still the purpose clause, for the third time in the level, and the plate is still the plain present.

words.note: 'Today', and it takes no ending ever. It joins L1-M4's caseless set: cotīdiē, crās, herī, hodiē — four words that never decline.
'The Saturnalia' — the December festival, and it is PLURAL with no singular at all: Sāturnālia sunt, never est. Latin has a small set of festival names like this.
'They are' — sum, es, est, sunt. Plural, because Sāturnālia is plural and has no singular to agree with instead.

sentences.trap: sunt, not est. Sāturnālia is plural and there is no singular of it anywhere in Latin — so the verb has no choice, and a learner who reads it as one festival and writes est has made an error the word itself cannot warn them about.
sentences.sound: ho-di-Ē sā-tur-NĀ-li-a SUNT. Nine syllables, and the long ē of hodiē and the long ā of the festival are the only lengths.

words.note: 'Today', and it takes no ending ever. It joins L1-M4's caseless set: cotīdiē, crās, herī, hodiē — four words that never decline.
'Day' — diēs as the subject. diēs nātālis is a birthday, literally 'the day of being born'.
'Of birth' — an adjective agreeing with diēs. English 'natal' and 'native' come from it, and so does 'Nativity'.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: A birthday is 'the day of being born', two words with the second agreeing with the first — and nātālis is M2's two-shape family, so it looks the same for a man or a woman and tells you nothing about whose birthday it is. That has to come from somewhere else in the sentence.

sentences.cue: It is the custom to give gifts.

words.note: 'Custom, habit' — mōs as the subject. mōs est plus an infinitive is 'it is the custom to'. English 'moral' comes from its plural, mōrēs.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'A gift' — dōnum for one, dōna for more than one. Neuter, so nothing changes between subject and object. English 'donate' and 'donor' keep it.
'To give' — dā's infinitive. L1-M8 taught dā, 'give!', and this is the same verb with nothing commanded.

sentences.trap: mōs est plus an infinitive is M7's melius est frame with a noun in front instead of a comparative. Nothing here is new grammar — the shape was built two modules ago, and a ninth module should be spending its cap on the nouns.
sentences.sound: MŌS EST DŌ-na DA-re. Two long ō sounds at the front and two short a syllables at the back.

sentences.usage: Said explaining what people do here.

sentences.cue: The Saturnalia is today; we are giving gifts.

words.note: 'The Saturnalia' — the December festival, and it is PLURAL with no singular at all: Sāturnālia sunt, never est. Latin has a small set of festival names like this.
'Today', and it takes no ending ever. It joins L1-M4's caseless set: cotīdiē, crās, herī, hodiē — four words that never decline.
'They are' — plural, because the festival is.
'A gift' — dōnum for one, dōna for more than one. Neuter, so nothing changes between subject and object. English 'donate' and 'donor' keep it.
'We give' — L1-M8's dā as a first-person plural: damus, dat, dant, dare. L2-M6's -mus ending on the shortest verb in the module.

sentences.trap: Two plurals for two different reasons. Sāturnālia is plural because the word has no singular; damus is plural because there is more than one of us. Nothing in the sentence connects them, and reading the second off the first is the mistake.

variations.cue: The Saturnalia is tomorrow; we are giving gifts.

sentences.usage: Said in the middle of a festival.

words.note: 'The Romans' — rōmānus for one, rōmānī for more than one. L1-M1's word, and here they are the people whose festival this is.
'The Saturnalia' — the December festival, and it is PLURAL with no singular at all: Sāturnālia sunt, never est. Latin has a small set of festival names like this.
'They do, they keep' — L1-M2's agō, and with a festival it means to hold or celebrate one. agō, agis, agit, agimus, agunt.

sentences.trap: The festival in this module is the ROMANS'. This course teaches one lexicon and coins nothing, and the source that gave it a telephone and a bicycle has no word for Diwali or Christmas Eve — so the culture here is Roman, and the module says so rather than pretending a Latin word exists for your own December.
sentences.sound: rō-MĀ-nī sā-tur-NĀ-li-a A-gunt. Three long ā sounds in a row across the two long words.

sentences.usage: Said describing whose custom it is.

sentences.cue: It is the custom not to work today.

words.note: 'Custom, habit' — mōs as the subject. mōs est plus an infinitive is 'it is the custom to'. English 'moral' comes from its plural, mōrēs.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'Today', and it takes no ending ever. It joins L1-M4's caseless set: cotīdiē, crās, herī, hodiē — four words that never decline.
'Not', and it denies the INFINITIVE: what is customary is not-working. M8's rule about where nōn belongs.
'To work' — labōrō's infinitive. M2's shape.

sentences.trap: nōn goes in front of labōrāre and not in front of est. Mōs nōn est labōrāre would say 'working is not the custom', which is nearly the same thing and not the same sentence — and M7 and M8 both spent a plate on this, which is why this one does not.

variations.cue: It is the custom not to read today.
variations.changed: a different thing not done

variations.cue: It is the custom to give gifts today.
variations.changed: a positive custom

variations.cue: I am not working today.
variations.changed: a fact about me rather than a custom

words.note: 'What', asking, and the object of agunt here. L1-M2's word.
'Today', and it takes no ending ever. It joins L1-M4's caseless set: cotīdiē, crās, herī, hodiē — four words that never decline.
'They do' — L1-M2's agō in the they-shape. quid agis? was 'how are you?'; quid agunt? is a real question about activity.

sentences.trap: quid agis? in L1-M2 meant 'how are you?' and quid hodiē agunt? means 'what are they doing?'. Same verb, same question word, and the idiom in the second person is not the literal question — which is worth knowing before you use the phrase on somebody else.

variations.changed: a named subject

sentences.usage: Said asking about a day's plans.
sentences.mnemonic: quid agis is an idiom; quid agunt is a question.

sentences.cue: He says it is the custom to give gifts.

words.note: 'He says' — dīcō, dīcit, dīxit. M5's verb.
'Custom' in the OBJECT shape, because the clause is reported: mōs as a subject, mōrem inside a report.
'To be' — sum's infinitive. M3 opened it.
'A gift' — dōnum for one, dōna for more than one. Neuter, so nothing changes between subject and object. English 'donate' and 'donor' keep it.
'To give' — dā's infinitive.

sentences.trap: Two infinitives in one reported clause and they are doing different things. esse is the reported clause's own verb and dare is what the custom IS — so the sentence is 'he says the-custom to-be to-give-gifts', which is three verbs deep and every one of them a shape the level has taught.
sentences.sound: DĪ-cit MŌ-rem ES-se DŌ-na DA-re. Three long vowels, one in each of the first three words.

sentences.usage: Said passing on what you were told about a place.

sentences.display: Ad Sāturnālia eō ut dōna dem.
sentences.cue: I am going to the Saturnalia in order to give gifts.
sentences.literal: to Saturnalia I-go so-that gifts I-may-give

words.note: 'To', with the object shape after it. L1-M4's preposition — and Sāturnālia is neuter plural, so it looks unchanged.
'The Saturnalia' — the December festival, and it is PLURAL with no singular at all: Sāturnālia sunt, never est. Latin has a small set of festival names like this.
'I go': eō, īs, it, īmus, īre.
'So that' — with a subjunctive, and the purpose reading only. M4's word.
'A gift' — dōnum for one, dōna for more than one. Neuter, so nothing changes between subject and object. English 'donate' and 'donor' keep it.
'That I may give' — dā's present subjunctive. M4's mood on L1-M8's verb, and another -am ending that could have been a future.

sentences.trap: Sāturnālia looks unchanged after ad, and it is the accusative — neuter plurals are identical in both cases, which M8 said about pretium. So a learner watching endings sees nothing and the preposition is the only evidence the case changed at all.

variations.display: Ad Sāturnālia it ut dōna det.
variations.cue: He is going to the Saturnalia to give gifts.
variations.changed: someone else, so both verbs move

variations.cue: I am going to the Saturnalia.
variations.changed: no purpose clause, so no mood

variations.display: Crās ad Sāturnālia eō ut dōna dem.

mistake.display: Ad Sāturnālia eō ut dōna dō.
mistake.why: the plain present after ut, for the third time in this level. A purpose clause is always subjunctive, and by the ninth module the plate is here not because the rule is new but because the sentences are long enough to lose it in.

words.note: 'Today', and it takes no ending ever. It joins L1-M4's caseless set: cotīdiē, crās, herī, hodiē — four words that never decline.
'The Saturnalia' — the December festival, and it is PLURAL with no singular at all: Sāturnālia sunt, never est. Latin has a small set of festival names like this.
'They are' — plural, because the festival is.
'Custom, habit' — mōs as the subject. mōs est plus an infinitive is 'it is the custom to'. English 'moral' comes from its plural, mōrēs.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'A gift' — dōnum for one, dōna for more than one. Neuter, so nothing changes between subject and object. English 'donate' and 'donor' keep it.
'To give' — dā's infinitive.
'And'. L1-M1's word, joining two infinitives here rather than two nouns.
'Not', denying the second infinitive only. The custom is to give AND not to work.
'To work' — labōrō's infinitive.

sentences.trap: Two infinitives joined by et and only the second one negated. The custom is to give gifts and not to work — so nōn belongs to labōrāre alone, and putting it before dare would negate both, which is a different holiday entirely.
